title: A global mandate threshold and unique closed-form optimum with foreign entry
scope: Global policy optimization in the source's monopoly local-content benchmark, sharpening its local learning-benefit condition.
significance: Proves g>delta/2 is globally necessary and sufficient for a beneficial positive mandate under strict baseline entry, and derives the unique optimum truncated by entry.
body:
# Global mandate threshold and a unique closed-form optimum

The source proves that \(g>\delta/2\) is sufficient for a locally beneficial mandate when baseline entry is strict. In its declared benchmark, that threshold is also globally necessary. Moreover the conditional-on-entry welfare curve is unimodal whenever a positive mandate can help, so its optimum can be written explicitly and then truncated by the entry constraint.

Let \(m=A-1>0\), \(\delta=c_0-1>0\), and use the source's \(\kappa\ge0\). On the positive-output region \(0\le\ell<m/\delta\),
\[
8W(\ell)=\frac{m^2+b\ell+c\ell^2}{1+\kappa\ell^2},
\quad
b=m(4g-2\delta),\quad c=\delta(\delta-4g).
\tag{A}
\]
This is obtained by combining the two terms of equation (2), rather than changing its ownership boundary. Put \(C=c-\kappa m^2\). Subtracting baseline welfare gives
\[
8\{W(\ell)-W(0)\}
=\frac{\ell(b+C\ell)}{1+\kappa\ell^2}.
\tag{B}
\]

If \(g\le\delta/2\), then \(b\le0\). If \(c\le0\), also \(C\le0\), and (B) is strictly negative for positive feasible output. If \(c>0\), use \(\ell<m/\delta\) to obtain
\[
b+C\ell\le b+c\ell<b+cm/\delta=-m\delta<0.
\]
Thus no positive mandate with entry can improve national welfare. An exit policy has welfare zero and cannot beat the positive-output baseline. This proves global necessity, including \(g=\delta/2\), where the first derivative vanishes but every positive mandate is still worse.

If \(g>\delta/2\), then \(b>0\), \(c<0\) and \(C<0\). Differentiating (A), the sign of \(W'\) is the sign of
\[
N(\ell)=b+2C\ell-\kappa b\ell^2.
\tag{C}
\]
For every \(\ell\ge0\), \(N'(\ell)=2C-2\kappa b\ell<0\), and \(N(0)=b>0\). It has exactly one positive zero. Hence welfare increases strictly until that zero and decreases strictly afterward. The unconstrained optimum is
\[
\ell_0=
\begin{cases}
-b/(2C),&\kappa=0,\\
b/(\sqrt{C^2+\kappa b^2}-C),&\kappa>0.
\end{cases}
\tag{D}
\]
The second expression is the rationalized positive quadratic root, avoiding cancellation. The root lies strictly below \(m/\delta\): welfare is positive at zero and tends to zero at the positive-output boundary, so its strictly unimodal maximum must precede that boundary.

Operating profit in equation (1) decreases strictly on the positive-output region. Its entry-supporting policies therefore form an initial interval. If baseline profit is strictly above \(F\), that interval contains a neighborhood of zero. The unique global policy optimum is the smaller of \(\ell_0\), one, and the positive-output entry boundary, whenever that boundary binds. At a positive-cost entry threshold the source's entry-at-equality convention includes the boundary. If \(F=0\), the output-zero boundary may be excluded from entry, but it cannot obstruct the interior maximizer in (D). Exit policies cannot improve upon the attained positive welfare maximum.

Thus, under strict baseline entry, a positive policy improvement exists if and only if \(g>\delta/2\). If baseline entry is exactly indifferent, every positive mandate can instead cause immediate exit; strict entry is essential to the sufficiency statement. If baseline profit is below \(F\), no mandate induces entry, by profit monotonicity.

This strengthens the source's one-dimensional numerical prescription into a global analytical solution for its specific procurement conduct and national ownership weights. It does not identify the learning parameter from sourcing data, compare subsidies with mandates under another equilibrium, or extend the threshold to competitive final production.

title: Sharp norm-ball price ambiguity and its interaction with strict positivity
scope: Exact Hilbert-space payoff-price ambiguity under a bounded discount-factor norm, with explicit positivity-qualified attainability and a fully computed three-state refinement.
significance: Replaces the source's generic 2M approximation bound by the exact residual-radius bound and characterizes its sharp positivity-truncated finite-state identified set.
body:
# Sharp norm-ball price ambiguity with strict positivity

The manuscript's affine characterization and its \(2M\epsilon\) approximate-spanning bound are correct. The latter can be tightened by removing the part of the factor norm already fixed by pricing restrictions. In the unrestricted norm-ball subclass, this gives an exact price interval before positivity, and explicit conditions for retaining exactness after positivity.

Let \(V\subset H=L^2(P)\) be the source's closed traded-and-instrumented span. Every solution of the linear pricing equations has the same projection \(m_V\) onto \(V\). Restrict the admissible class further by \(\|m\|_2\le M\). Ignoring positivity temporarily, every feasible factor has the orthogonal decomposition
\[
m=m_V+h,\quad h\in V^\perp,\quad
\|h\|_2\le r:=\sqrt{M^2-\|m_V\|_2^2}.
\tag{A}
\]
If \(M<\|m_V\|_2\), the norm-restricted linear class is empty. If \(M=\|m_V\|_2\), it contains only \(m_V\), which may or may not satisfy positivity.

For any payoff \(f\in H\), put \(f_\perp=f-\Pi_Vf\). Orthogonality gives
\[
E[mf]=\langle m_V,f\rangle+\langle h,f_\perp\rangle.
\]
Hence the exact unrestricted-norm-ball price interval is
\[
\left[\langle m_V,f\rangle-r\|f_\perp\|_2,\ 
      \langle m_V,f\rangle+r\|f_\perp\|_2\right].
\tag{B}
\]
Cauchy–Schwarz proves inclusion. If \(f_\perp\ne0\), choosing \(h=\pm r f_\perp/\|f_\perp\|_2\) attains both endpoints; scalar multiples attain every intermediate point. When \(f_\perp=0\), the interval is a singleton, as required for a traded payoff.

Strictly positive factors form a subset of this ball, so their price diameter is at most \(2r\,{\rm dist}(f,V)\), improving the source's \(2M\,{\rm dist}(f,V)\). Positivity need not allow either extremizer in (B), and a norm-ball result should not silently claim that it does. A sufficient condition for full closed-interval sharpness is
\[
m_V\ge c>0,\qquad
f_\perp\in L^\infty,\qquad
r\|f_\perp\|_\infty/\|f_\perp\|_2<c.
\tag{C}
\]
Then both extremizers, and the whole segment between them, remain strictly positive. Without this interior margin, endpoints can be deleted or the interval can shrink further.

The source's three-state example makes that qualification concrete. Its full positive set is
\[
m=(1+a,1-2a,1+a),\qquad -1<a<1/2,
\]
under equal state probabilities. The identified projection is \(m_V=(1,1,1)\), since \((1,-2,1)\) is orthogonal to both the risk-free return and the risky return \((0,1,2)\). Direct calculation gives
\[
\|m\|_2^2=1+2a^2.
\]
Therefore the exact additional norm restriction is
\[
a\in(-1,1/2)\cap[-s,s],\qquad
s=\sqrt{(M^2-1)/2},
\tag{D}
\]
when \(M\ge1\). For the source's payoff \(f=(1,0,1)\), the sharp price set is precisely the affine image \(\{2(1+a)/3:a\text{ satisfies (D)}\}\). Every point is attained by its displayed positive factor.

For \(1\le M<\sqrt{3/2}\), both endpoints \(\pm s\) lie inside the positivity range, so the interval is closed. At \(M=\sqrt{3/2}\), the upper endpoint \(a=1/2\) is excluded by strict positivity. At \(M=\sqrt3\), the lower endpoint \(a=-1\) is excluded as well. For larger \(M\), the original open price interval \((0,1)\) is recovered. If \(M<1\), no factor exists; this also follows from \(E[m]=1\) and Jensen's inequality.

This is an exact identified-set refinement within the stated population model. It does not provide a statistical recovery procedure, certify empirical completeness, or make the nontraded component economically unique merely by selecting a minimum-norm factor. No external reference is needed for the derivation.

title: A larger indexation spread can accompany a higher pricing premium
scope: Comparative statics and exact boundary example in the source's two-state log-utility sovereign contract family with nonnegative repayments.
significance: Shows that a pricing premium can increase the optimal spread by relaxing the low-payment boundary, despite reducing interior insurance incentives; supplies exact admissible contracts and welfare comparison.
body:
# A larger optimal spread can accompany a higher pricing premium

The manuscript's adoption and optimum formulas are correct. They also reveal a potentially misleading comparative static: an increase in the ambiguity-plus-liquidity premium can increase the chosen repayment spread. The interior optimum moves in the opposite direction, but nonnegative repayment constraints can dominate. This is a boundary phenomenon inside the source's fixed-funding model.

Write \(q=1-p\), \(a=q-\kappa>0\), \(b=p+\kappa\), and \(x_s=y_s-B\). For fixed spread \(d\), the marginal expected utility is
\[
V_\kappa'(d)=\frac{pa}{x_L+ad}-\frac{qb}{x_H-bd}.
\]
Differentiating this marginal utility with respect to \(\kappa\), while keeping \(d\) fixed, gives
\[
\partial_\kappa V_\kappa'(d)
=-\frac{px_L}{(x_L+ad)^2}
-\frac{qx_H}{(x_H-bd)^2}<0.
\tag{A}
\]
Strict concavity then implies that a feasible interior optimum decreases with the premium. The adoption condition can also be written
\[
\kappa<
\frac{pq(x_H-x_L)}{px_H+qx_L}.
\tag{B}
\]
Thus the premium weakens the marginal incentive to introduce insurance.

Nevertheless, nonnegative low-state repayment requires
\[
g_L=B-ad\ge0,\qquad d\le B/a.
\tag{C}
\]
Unlike the interior optimum and the incentive bound, this upper bound increases with \(\kappa\). If it binds, the optimal spread may increase.

Here is an exact example. Take \(p=q=1/2\), \((y_L,y_H)=(3,7)\), \(B=1\), and \(k_H=\log10\). Impose no additional repayment caps. First set \(\kappa=0\). Then \(a=b=1/2\), \((x_L,x_H)=(2,6)\), and the unconstrained optimum is
\[
d_{\rm unc}=
\frac{pa x_H-qb x_L}{ab}=4.
\]
The nonnegative-payment bound is two. The truth-telling bound is \(54/(1+9/2)=108/11>2\), so the unique optimum is \(d^*=2\). It gives repayments \((0,2)\), consumptions \((3,5)\), and expected utility \(\tfrac12\log15\).

Now increase the premium to \(\kappa=1/20\). Choose the source's ambiguity component equal to zero and liquidity coefficient \(1/20\), so the interval restriction on lender probabilities is satisfied. We have
\[
a=9/20,\quad b=11/20,\quad
d_{\rm unc}=320/99,\quad B/a=20/9.
\]
The incentive bound is \(54/(1+99/20)=1080/119>20/9\). Since \(320/99>20/9\), the unique optimum is \(d^*=20/9\), strictly larger than two. Its repayments and consumptions are
\[
(g_L,g_H)=(0,20/9),\qquad
(c_L,c_H)=(3,43/9).
\]
Pricing checks exactly:
\[
\tfrac12(20/9)-\tfrac1{20}(20/9)=1=B.
\]
Both consumptions are positive, and high-state truth-telling holds by the computed incentive bound. The low-state false report demands a larger payment and cannot improve utility, as in the source.

Expected utility now equals \(\tfrac12\log(43/3)\), strictly below \(\tfrac12\log15\). The larger spread therefore does not indicate better insurance or welfare: low-state consumption is unchanged, while the increased spread finances the premium by lowering high-state consumption. Measuring contract contingency solely by \(d\) would miss this distinction.

Equation (A) explains the interior force, while (C) explains why clipping the optimum can reverse its sign. The source makes no blanket monotonicity claim, so this is a substantive comparative-static caution, not an error finding. It retains no default, fixed proceeds, log utility, fixed output probabilities and exogenous reporting costs. Dynamic default, endogenous issuance and the resource cost of verification remain outside the calculation.
